newsitem.title: INDIA: India could ease oil importer's borrowing - analysts.
newsitem.headline: India could ease oil importer's borrowing - analysts.

text.p: The Indian government, reluctant to increase petroleum prices to plug a ballooning deficit, might instead opt to ease a restriction on Indian Oil Corp's overseas borrowing, analysts said on Thursday.
But over the longer term, pressure will mount on the government unless it raises petroleum product prices to bridge a gap between domestic and international levels, they said.
Currently the government owes about 190 billion rupees ($5.32 billion) to oil companies for selling refined product below market prices to support the country's subsidy regime.
About 60 percent of the debt is owed to state-controlled IOC, which imports oil and petroleum products on behalf of the government.
The debt to the companies ballooned when world oil prices surged late last year and India left its prices unchanged.
The government has repeatedly put off a decision on whether to increase the prices of some petroleum products.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, heading a fragile centre-left coalition, was quoted in newspapers this week as saying prices would be raised in mid-August.
But analysts said there was growing speculation the government, facing stiff opposition from leftwing allies and the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party, would put off a price hike.
It might instead raise the limit on external commercial borrowing (ECB) by IOC, permitting it to pay for imports.

"The government has lost the political will. And there is a crisis brewing within the ruling Janata Dal party," said an analyst with a Bombay-based securities firm. "The softer option will be to hike the ECB."
Avdhoot Sabnis, an analyst with James Capel, said: "The obvious choice will be to raise the ECB limit. This route has been the most preferred one for the last one year."

The Finance Ministry raised state-run IOC's ECB limit to $2.02 billion in February 1996 from $1.5 billion. Subsequently, the limit was raised to $2.5 billion in November 1996 and to $2.9 billion in February 1997.
"With a provision of raising foreign currency non-resident loans of $600 million, IOC's cumulative limit is $3.5 billion," an IOC spokesman said.
"IOC's borrowing currently stands below $3 billion but it will touch the $3.5-billion limit in September."

The IOC spokesman said the limit could be raised any number of times. "The other option could be to reduce the private sector's share of ECB while keeping the overall limit intact," said the analyst with the Bombay firm.
Over the longer term, there is no option but to raise prices since the state will owe oil companies 245 billion rupees by the end of 1997/98 (April/March) if prices are not adjusted, analysts said.

A committee, set up to suggest reforms in the hydrocarbon sector, has recommended a "soft-landing" approach which would include the removal of a subsidy on diesel and the reduction of subsidies on kerosene, liquefied petroleum gas and input for fertilisers by 1998.
That would be followed by a subsequent reduction of subsidies and eventual total deregulation by 2002, the committee has recommended.
